01.note: A cow from the household of Menahem had its womb removed. Rabbi Tarfon ruled that the injury would kill it and that it was forbidden as food, so the owner fed it to the dogs. Later the Sages at Yavne ruled such a cow permitted, because Theodosius the doctor reported that cows and pigs are never allowed out of Alexandria in Egypt until their wombs have been cut out. Rabbi Tarfon cried, "Your donkey is gone, Tarfon," expecting to have to pay for the cow. Rabbi Akiva told him he was exempt, because any judge accepted as an expert by the public does not have to pay for his mistakes.
01.why: Rav Sheshet has said a judge's ruling is revoked if he forgot an explicit teaching, but stands if he erred in weighing opinions. Rav Hamnuna raises this case against him: why did Rabbi Akiva not simply say Tarfon's ruling was void? The Gemara answers that Akiva gave both reasons.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage who ruled the cow forbidden and then feared he owed its owner the cost of it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells Rabbi Tarfon he does not have to pay.

people.name: Theodosius the doctor
people.about: A physician whose report on the cattle of Alexandria led the Sages at Yavne to permit the cow.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: Raises this incident as an objection to Rav Sheshet.

terms.meaning: An animal with an injury or defect that will kill it within a year. Its meat is forbidden to eat even if it is slaughtered properly.
A town where the Sages held their court and study house.
A judge whom the community has accepted as qualified to rule. If he rules wrongly in good faith, he is not liable to pay for the loss.

02.note: Some hooligans lived in Rabbi Zeira's neighborhood. He treated them as friends so that they would repent, and the other Sages disapproved. When Rabbi Zeira died, the hooligans said: until now the short one with the singed legs prayed for compassion for us; who will pray for us now? They thought this over in their hearts and repented.
02.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Zeira's reading of a verse: even the traitors and sinners among the Jewish people carry some goodness. The story shows him living by that belief, and his hope for the sinners being borne out.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who befriended the hooligans next door so that they would repent, against the other Sages' wishes.

03.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah swore that he once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran after them and found the man holding a sword dripping with blood, with the victim convulsing on the ground. He said to him: Wicked man, who killed this man, you or I? But I cannot do anything to you, because the Torah requires two witnesses for a death sentence, and I did not see you kill him. The One Who knows thoughts will punish you. The Sages said that before they left the spot, a snake came and bit the killer, and he died.
03.why: A teaching has just said that a witness who saw only a chase, a bloody sword and a dying man has seen nothing and cannot testify to the murder. This case shows that rule at work. The Gemara then asks why a murderer would die from a snakebite.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: Sees a killer with a bloody sword over his victim but cannot have him put to death without two witnesses to the killing itself.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law. The Gemara often quotes one as evidence.

04.note: Yehuda and Hizkiyya, the young sons of Rabbi Hiyya, sat at a meal with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said nothing. Rabbi told his servants to give them more wine so that they would talk. Once they were drunk, they said that the Messiah will not come until two families in Israel are destroyed: the family of the head of the exile in Babylonia, and the family of the Nasi in the Land of Israel, which was Rabbi's own. Rabbi said: My children, are you throwing thorns in my eyes? Their father, Rabbi Hiyya, asked him not to take offense. The word for wine and the word for secret both add up to seventy in Hebrew letters, he said: when wine goes in, secrets come out.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabbi Hiyya who says, once drunk, what he had kept quiet about.

people.name: Hizkiyya
people.about: Yehuda's brother, also a son of Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi. He is the host of the meal and the Nasi whose family the young men name.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hizkiyya. He defends his sons to Rabbi.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel. The office passed down within one family.
The leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia, also called the Exilarch.
The Messiah, the future king descended from King David.

05.note: The Roman emperor told Rabban Gamliel that his God is a thief, because He put Adam to sleep and took one of his ribs. The emperor's daughter said she would answer. She asked her father for an officer, because bandits had come in the night, taken a silver jug and left a gold one. He said he wished such bandits would come every day. She said that this was just what happened to Adam: a rib was taken and he was given a wife to serve him. The emperor answered that God should have done it openly. She had raw meat brought, roasted it under the embers and offered it to him, and he said it disgusted him. So too, she said, Adam would have been disgusted by Eve if he had watched her being taken from him.
05.why: The Gemara is collecting replies to challenges against verses of the Torah. Just before this, a launderer answers a heretic on Rabbi Yishmael's behalf; here the emperor's daughter answers her father for Rabban Gamliel in the same way.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage the emperor challenges.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who calls God a thief.

people.name: the emperor's daughter
people.about: She answers her father's challenge for Rabban Gamliel.

06.note: The emperor told Rabban Gamliel that it was nothing great for God to count the stars, since he could count them too. Rabban Gamliel put quinces in a sieve, spun it and told him to count them. The emperor asked him to hold them still, and Rabban Gamliel said the sky turns in the same way. In another version, the emperor claimed to have counted the stars. Rabban Gamliel asked him how many teeth he had, and the emperor put his hand in his mouth to count them. Rabban Gamliel said: you do not know what is in your own mouth, and you know what is in the sky?
06.why: This is one in a run of exchanges between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel. Just before, the emperor claimed to know where God sits and was told he does not even know where his own son is.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's boast.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who claims he can count the stars.

07.note: The emperor invited Rabbi Tanhum to make Jews and Romans into one people. Rabbi Tanhum agreed, but said that circumcised Jews could not become uncircumcised, so the Romans should be circumcised and become like them. The emperor said the argument was a good one, but anyone who defeats the king in argument is thrown to the wild animals. Rabbi Tanhum was thrown in and the animals did not eat him. A heretic said this was only because they were not hungry. Then the heretic was thrown in, and the animals ate him.
07.why: This belongs to a series of debates between Sages and a Roman emperor, heretics or a Persian priest about God and the Jewish people.

people.name: Rabbi Tanhum
people.about: The Sage who wins his argument with the emperor and survives the wild animals.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who proposes one people and then throws Rabbi Tanhum to the animals.

people.name: a certain heretic
people.about: Says the animals were not hungry, and is eaten by them himself.

terms.meaning: A pen holding wild animals. People thrown into it were meant to be killed by the animals.

08.note: The emperor mocked Rabban Gamliel: the Jews say the Divine Presence rests wherever ten of them gather, so how many Divine Presences are there? Rabban Gamliel called over the emperor's servant, struck him on the neck, and asked why he had let the sun into the emperor's house. The emperor said that the sun shines on the whole world. Rabban Gamliel answered that if the sun, only one of countless servants before God, shines on the whole world, then the Divine Presence of God certainly does.
08.why: This is another in the run of exchanges between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel and other Sages, each answering a challenge to Jewish belief about God.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's mockery with the example of the sun.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who mocks the idea of the Divine Presence.

people.name: the emperor's servant
people.about: Struck by Rabban Gamliel to set up his answer.

terms.meaning: God's presence as it rests in a particular place or among people.

09.note: A teaching reports that on the eve of Passover they hung the corpse of Jesus the Nazarene. For forty days beforehand a crier went out announcing that he was going to be stoned for sorcery, for inciting people to worship idols and for leading the Jewish people astray, and calling on anyone who knew a reason to acquit him to come forward. No one found a reason to acquit him, so they stoned him and hung his corpse on Passover eve.
09.why: The mishna says a crier goes out only as the condemned man is led to execution. This teaching seems to contradict it, since here the crier went out forty days early. Ulla answers that Jesus was a special case: he had close ties to the government, so the court gave him every chance.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: Here, a man condemned for sorcery and leading the Jewish people astray. He was stoned and his corpse hung on Passover eve.

terms.meaning: An official who announced in public who was being executed and for what, so that anyone with evidence for the accused could come forward.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

10.note: A teaching says that Jesus the Nazarene had five disciples: Mattai, Nakai, Netzer, Buni and Toda. They were brought to trial one at a time. Each pleaded for his life with a verse that plays on his own name, and the judges answered each one with another verse on the same name, saying that he should be executed. The text does not say what then happened to them.
10.why: The Gemara has just discussed the trial of Jesus. It adds this second teaching about his disciples, and then Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi expounds the last verse quoted, about the thanks-offering.

people.name: Mattai
people.about: A disciple of Jesus who pleads with a verse containing the word matai, "when."

people.name: Nakai
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about the innocent, naki.

people.name: Netzer
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about a branch, netzer.

people.name: Buni
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about a firstborn son, beni.

people.name: Toda
people.about: A disciple who pleads with a verse about thanksgiving, toda.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

11.note: A man was being taken out to be executed. He said: if I committed this sin, let my death not atone for any of my sins; if I did not, let it atone for all of them. The court and all Israel are clear, he said, but the witnesses will never be forgiven. When the Sages heard this, they said that he could not be brought back for retrial, because the sentence had already been passed. He would be executed, and the guilt for his death would hang around the necks of the witnesses.
11.why: The mishna has just ruled that a condemned man may not publicly declare himself innocent, so as not to cast blame on the court and the witnesses. The Gemara then asks why this case needed saying, and answers that he is executed even when the witnesses take back their testimony.

terms.meaning: Being cleared of sin before God. The Sages taught that a condemned man's death, together with his confession, atones for his sins.

12.note: In the days of Greek rule, a man rode a horse on the Sabbath. He was brought to court and stoned, not because he deserved it, but because the times required it. In another case, a man had intercourse with his wife in public under a fig tree. He was brought to court and flogged, again not because he deserved it, but because the times required it.
12.why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov has just taught that a court may impose lashes and death even where Torah law does not require them, as a fence to keep people from sin. These two cases are his examples.

terms.meaning: The Sages' phrase for an emergency measure. A court could punish more harshly than the law prescribes when people had grown lax in some area.
The period when Greek rulers governed the Land of Israel.

13.note: Imrata bat Talei, a priest's daughter, committed adultery. Rav Hama bar Toviyya surrounded her with bundles of branches and burned her. Rav Yosef said he made two mistakes. First, Rav Mattana had taught that burning is carried out with a wick of lead. Second, a teaching from the verse about coming before the priests and the judge says that capital cases may be judged only when priests serve in the Temple.
13.why: The Gemara is explaining how execution by burning is carried out. Right after this, it turns to the mishna's report of another priest's daughter burned with branches.

people.name: Imrata bat Talei
people.about: A priest's daughter who committed adultery and was burned.

people.name: Rav Hama bar Toviyya
people.about: The judge who had her burned with branches.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Says Rav Hama bar Toviyya made two mistakes.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: His ruling that burning is done with a lead wick is cited against Rav Hama bar Toviyya.

terms.meaning: The method the Sages describe for execution by burning: molten lead poured down the throat, rather than burning the body in a fire.
The Torah singles out a priest's daughter who commits adultery for death by burning.

14.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, reported a case of a priest's daughter who committed adultery and was put to death by actual burning. The Sages told him the court at that time was not expert in the law. Rav Yosef said that it was a court of Sadducees.
14.why: The discussion has just faulted Rav Hama bar Toviyya for burning a priest's daughter with branches. It now turns to the mishna's similar report, and Rav Yosef explains why a court would have done it that way.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Reports the burning of a priest's daughter to the Sages.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Says the court in that case was a court of Sadducees.

terms.meaning: A Jewish group that rejected the Sages' traditions and read the Torah literally. Here, they took the burning literally.
A passage of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

14.flag: The STORY segment only quotes the opening of the mishna's report, cut short with "etc.", plus Rav Yosef's one-line comment; the events themselves appear only in the translator's gloss.

15.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, remembered riding on his father's shoulders as a child when a priest's daughter who had committed adultery was brought out, surrounded with bundles of branches and burned. The Sages told him that he had been a minor then, and that a minor's testimony cannot be used as proof.
15.why: In the mishna's version the Sages dismissed his report by saying the court was not expert. The Gemara asks how both versions can be right, answers that there were two separate incidents, and then works out which one he told first.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Remembers seeing a priest's daughter burned when he was a child on his father's shoulders.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of legal responsibility. The Sages did not accept a minor's testimony as proof.

16.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta was walking along a road when lions came at him, roaring. He quoted the verse, "The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their food from God." Two thighs of meat came down from heaven. The lions ate one and left the other. He took it to the study hall and asked whether it was kosher. The Sages told him that nothing non-kosher comes down from heaven.
16.why: The Gemara has claimed that Adam was not allowed to eat meat. When a teaching says angels roasted meat for him, the Gemara answers that this was meat from heaven. It then asks whether such meat exists, and this story is the proof that it does.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta
people.about: Meets roaring lions on the road and is given meat from heaven.

terms.meaning: The house of study where the Sages met to learn and to decide questions of Jewish law.
Permitted to eat under Jewish law.

17.note: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name a story about a gentile woman who was very ill. She vowed that if she recovered, she would worship every idol in the world. She recovered and did so. When she reached Peor, she asked its priests how it was worshipped. They told her: you eat spinach and drink beer, and then defecate before it. She said she would rather fall ill again than worship an idol that way.
17.why: Rav Yehuda draws the lesson right after: the Jewish people were not like her, and the verse says they attached themselves tightly to Ba'al-Peor. A teaching that follows reads the same verse the opposite way.

people.name: a certain gentile woman
people.about: Vows to worship every idol if she recovers, but refuses to worship Peor.

terms.meaning: Ba'al-Peor, an idol the Torah mentions. It was worshipped by defecating before it.

18.note: Sabbeta ben Alas, a Jew, rented out his donkey to a gentile woman. When she reached Peor, she asked him to wait while she went in. When she came out, he asked her to wait while he went in. She said: aren't you Jewish? He said: what do you care? He went in, defecated before the idol and wiped himself on its nose. The priests of Peor praised him, saying no one had ever worshipped it so well.
18.why: The ruling that follows says that one who defecates before Ba'al-Peor has worshipped it, even if he meant to insult it. This story shows how an insult can turn into worship.

people.name: Sabbeta ben Alas
people.about: A Jew who rents out his donkey to a gentile woman and tries to insult the idol Peor.

people.name: a certain gentile woman
people.about: Hires Sabbeta's donkey and goes to worship at Peor.

terms.meaning: Ba'al-Peor, an idol the Torah mentions. It was worshipped by defecating before it.

19.note: Rav Menashe was traveling to Bei Torta. People told him an idol stood there, so he picked up a stone and threw it at it. They told him it was Mercury, an idol worshipped by throwing stones. He said that the mishna makes a person liable only for throwing a stone as worship. He went to the study hall to ask. The Sages told him one is liable even when he means to stone it as an insult. He offered to go and take the stone back. They told him that both taking a stone away and adding one make a person liable, since each stone taken away leaves space for another.
19.why: The Gemara has just ruled that throwing a stone at Mercury counts as worship even if the thrower meant to insult it. Here a Sage learns that ruling the hard way.

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: A Sage who throws a stone at an idol to insult it, then asks the study hall whether he has sinned.

terms.meaning: A Roman idol worshipped by throwing stones onto a pile beside it.
A passage of the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, which the Sages quote and argue over.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and to decide questions of Jewish law.

20.note: Turnus Rufus, the wicked Roman governor, asked Rabbi Akiva what makes the Sabbath different from other days. Rabbi Akiva asked him what makes him more important than other men. Turnus Rufus said it was because his master, the emperor, wished it. Rabbi Akiva answered that the Sabbath is special because his Master, God, wished it. Turnus Rufus then asked how anyone knows which day is really the Sabbath. Rabbi Akiva said there were three proofs: the Sabbatyon River, which is calm only on the Sabbath; a necromancer, whose dead do not rise on the Sabbath; and the grave of Turnus Rufus's own father, which gives off smoke all week but not on the Sabbath. Turnus Rufus said: you have demeaned him, shamed him and cursed him.
20.why: A teaching has just said that the dead raised by one kind of necromancer do not rise on the Sabbath. The Gemara adds that Turnus Rufus put this same question to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: The Roman governor who challenges Rabbi Akiva about the Sabbath.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Answers Turnus Rufus and names his father's grave as proof.

terms.meaning: A river in Jewish legend that rages all week and rests on the Sabbath.
Someone who claims to call up the dead and ask them questions.
The place where the wicked are punished after death. Here, the smoke from the father's grave is a sign that he is being punished there.
